profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a university-affiliated environmental informatics lab two weeks into a summer alpine monitoring campaign. The team’s new real-time QC pipeline, based on a dynamic Bayesian network trained on prior SensorScope-style deployments, is generating an unusually high volume of anomaly flags and a backlog of imputed values after a thunderstorm event at the Montreux Ridge field site. The agenda is to diagnose why the live system is over-flagging and delaying downstream dashboards, determine whether the issue is due to sensor behavior, network outages, or model configuration, and agree on a practical fix that can be applied before the next field maintenance window. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan: what logs to inspect, what model or pipeline adjustments to make today, and what will count as the issue being fixed for this week’s operations.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Probabilistic modeling, Bayesian networks, sensor data QC, ecological time-series analysis
members.background: Maya leads the lab’s automated QC methods and adapted the spatiotemporal anomaly-detection model from prior watershed deployments to the current alpine campaign; she works mostly from archived data and cloud dashboards rather than field hardware.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve confidence in the model before an internal demo, avoid reverting to simpler rule-based QC, and show that the recent false alarms are likely due to deployment-specific configuration rather than a flaw in the modeling approach.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss a 'sensor failure,' they usually mean a bad observation stream that should be corrected or imputed, even if the physical device is still powered and reporting.
The 'storm period' relevant to troubleshooting is the post-cleaning event window beginning after the 06:00 automated daily baseline reset, because that is how the live QC jobs partition days.
If the team says the pipeline should be 'stable again,' that means anomaly rates and imputation latency return to the normal range seen on the operations dashboard over the next 24 hours.

Checking whether the site graph is 'updated' means rerunning structure adaptation using the existing site metadata and recent data, not physically re-auditing placement or antenna orientation in the field.

members.name: Ethan Ruiz
members.expertise: Wireless sensor deployments, telemetry reliability, station maintenance, embedded logging and calibration workflows
members.background: Ethan manages installation and maintenance for the Montreux Ridge network, including mast placement, battery systems, radio links, and periodic calibration swaps; he was on site the day after the storm and has practical knowledge of hardware behavior under exposure.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid unnecessary remote model tweaks that could mask a genuine hardware or topology issue, minimize risky changes before the next helicopter supply run, and protect the field team from being blamed for data artifacts caused by unrealistic model assumptions.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss a 'sensor failure,' they usually mean a physical or communication fault in the instrument chain, distinct from a mathematically unusual but still real environmental reading.
The 'storm period' relevant to troubleshooting is the full weather event starting when precipitation began around 23:40 local time, because exposure and radio degradation began then.
If the team says the pipeline should be 'stable again,' that means stations are no longer generating alarms that trigger field follow-up and the data stream can be trusted without manual triage.

Checking whether the site graph is 'updated' means confirming the deployed neighborhood relationships still match actual line-of-sight, mast relocation, and sensor replacement history at Montreux Ridge.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a sensor failure
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly discuss whether the model is confusing 'sensor failures' with valid observations.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats 'sensor failure' as any observation stream that is unreliable enough to be flagged and imputed, including drift, stuck values, or locally inconsistent readings from an otherwise functioning device.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats 'sensor failure' as a hardware, calibration, or communications fault in the physical sensing chain; a surprising but plausible microclimate reading is not a failure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this domain, both hardware faults and bad data are routinely talked about under the umbrella of 'sensor failure,' so the phrase feels standard and neither participant expects it to need unpacking during a troubleshooting call.

misalignment_points.topic: Which storm window they are analyzing
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the storm period' and 'that overnight event' while citing anomaly spikes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of records from 06:00 to 14:00 local time on the day after the storm, because the QC dashboard groups alerts by processing day and the morning spike is where the false-positive rate jumps.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the actual meteorological event beginning around 23:40 the previous night and continuing until dawn, because that is when icing, packet loss, and mast sway started.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are focused on the same real-world storm and use natural shorthand, but one indexes it by dashboard reporting window and the other by field event onset, so references appear aligned even while they compare different slices of data.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the issue should be 'stable again' or 'fixed for this week' before the next maintenance window.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the problem is fixed if alert volume, imputation lag, and downstream dashboard continuity return to baseline without degrading overall QC performance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the problem is fixed if the system stops producing alarms that imply urgent field intervention and operators can trust that flagged stations correspond to real equipment checks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria sound like operational stability and are compatible at a surface level, so they can agree on the same phrase while silently optimizing for different evidence of success.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to update the site graph
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'update the site graph' before rerunning the live QC model.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means rerunning the Bayesian structure-learning step with the latest month of data and existing station metadata, then redeploying the learned graph in software.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means manually verifying and editing neighborhood relationships to reflect actual station relocation, new wind shield installation, and radio visibility changes since deployment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine maintenance action tied to the same graph object, but each participant owns a different layer of the system and defaults to their own standard method without considering the other interpretation.
